edges.description: Endocytosis delivers the BoNT dichain into the endosomal lumen, where acidification drives the translocation step.
edges.source: Presynaptic Cholinergic Nerve Terminal Targeting and Endocytosis

edges.description: Released LC metalloprotease gains access to cytosolic SNARE proteins at the presynaptic membrane.
SNARE cleavage abolishes the molecular machinery for synaptic vesicle fusion, selectively blocking acetylcholine release at cholinergic synapses.
Loss of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions produces complete motor blockade and descending flaccid paralysis.

nodes.description: SNARE complex disruption prevents fusion of acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction and at autonomic cholinergic synapses. Vesicles accumulate but cannot release their contents, producing persistent blockade of acetylcholine transmission.

biological_processes: negative regulation of acetylcholine secretion, neurotransmission

evidence.reference_title: Botulinum toxin A inhibits acetylcholine release from cultured neurons in vitro.
evidence.snippet: Clostridium botulinum type toxin A (BoTx) blocks stimulus-induced acetylcholine (ACh) release from presynaptic nerve terminals at peripheral neuromuscular junctions.

nodes.description: Persistent blockade of acetylcholine release at motor nerve terminals and postganglionic parasympathetic synapses produces the characteristic syndrome: symmetrical, descending flaccid paralysis beginning with cranial nerve involvement (diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria) and progressing caudally to limb and trunk weakness; autonomic features (dry mouth, mydriasis, constipation, urinary retention) reflect parasympathetic blockade. Progressive respiratory muscle weakness may cause fatal apnea. Toxin type A causes the most severe syndrome with highest rates of ventilatory failure; recovery requires weeks to months via axonal sprouting and formation of new neuromuscular junctions.

evidence.snippet: Botulism is rare neuroparalytic disease caused by botulinum toxin, one of the most toxic substances known.

All forms of botulism manifest as a distinct clinical syndrome of symmetrical cranial nerve palsies followed by descending symmetrical flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles, which may progress to respiratory failure and death.

nodes.description: Endosomal acidification induces a pH-dependent conformational change in the heavy chain translocation domain, inserting it into the endosomal membrane to form a protein-conducting channel. The disulfide-linked light chain (LC) is translocated in an N-to-C-terminus orientation through this channel into the neuronal cytosol; reduction of the interchain disulfide bridge on the cytosolic face releases the LC as an active zinc-metalloprotease.

evidence.reference_title: Crucial role of the disulfide bridge between botulinum neurotoxin light and heavy chains in protease translocation across membranes.
evidence.snippet: Intoxication requires the disulfide-linked, di-chain protein to undergo conformational changes in response to pH and redox gradients across the endosomal membrane with consequent formation of a protein-conducting channel by the heavy chain (HC) that translocates the light chain (LC) protease into the cytosol.

nodes.description: The heavy chain (HC) of BoNT binds with high affinity to gangliosides accumulated on the plasma membrane and to protein receptors on synaptic vesicle membranes (SV2 for serotypes A and E; synaptotagmin for serotypes B and G) exposed during vesicle exocytosis. This dual-receptor interaction clusters BoNT at cholinergic nerve terminals and triggers receptor-mediated endocytosis into synaptic vesicle-enriched endosomes.

evidence.reference_title: Identification of the SV2 protein receptor-binding site of botulinum neurotoxin type E.
evidence.snippet: SV2 (synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2) mediates the uptake of BoNT/A and /E, whereas Syt (synaptotagmin) is responsible for the endocytosis of BoNT/B and /G.

evidence.reference_title: Botulinum Neurotoxins: History, Mechanism, and Applications. A Narrative Review
evidence.snippet: BoNTs consist of a heavy chain that mediates high-affinity neuronal binding and endocytosis, and a light chain that, once translocated into the cytosol, acts as a zinc-dependent metalloprotease.

nodes.description: The cytosolic light chain acts as a zinc-endopeptidase with strict serotype-specific SNARE substrate selectivity: serotypes A and E cleave SNAP-25; serotypes B, D, F, and G cleave VAMP/synaptobrevin; serotype C cleaves syntaxin and SNAP-25. Cleavage of any one SNARE component prevents assembly of the ternary SNARE complex required for synaptic vesicle membrane fusion, thereby blocking neurotransmitter exocytosis.

evidence.reference_title: Tetanus and botulinum-B neurotoxins block neurotransmitter release by proteolytic cleavage of synaptobrevin.
evidence.snippet: tetanus and botulinum toxins serotype B are zinc endopeptidases, the activation of which requires reduction of the interchain disulphide bond. The protease activity is localized on the light chain and is specific for synaptobrevin, an integral membrane protein of small synaptic vesicles.

evidence.reference_title: Toxicology and pharmacology of botulinum and tetanus neurotoxins: an update.
evidence.snippet: Tetanus and botulinum neurotoxins cause the neuroparalytic syndromes of tetanus and botulism, respectively, by delivering inside different types of neurons, metalloproteases specifically cleaving the SNARE proteins that are essential for the release of neurotransmitters.

evidence.reference_title: Botulinum Toxin: A Comprehensive Review of Its Molecular Architecture and Mechanistic Action
evidence.snippet: The toxin's mechanism of action involves a multi-step process: recognition, binding, and catalysis, ultimately blocking neurotransmitter release by cleaving proteins like SNAP-25, VAMP, and syntaxin.
